title: The Simulated Larger Network
takeaway: The figure states the paper's working picture of superposition: the network we can actually inspect is a squeezed-down projection of a much larger, much sparser network whose neurons would each be one clean feature. Because that projection packs more feature directions than there are neurons, the directions can only be almost orthogonal rather than orthogonal, and a single real neuron ends up sitting on several feature directions at once — which is what polysemanticity looks like from the neuron's point of view.
walkthrough:
You are looking at two cartoon networks stacked one above the other, with three orange dashed arrows running from the top one to the bottom one, and three lines of explanatory text down the right side.

### The two panels

The top panel is labelled HYPOTHETICAL DISENTANGLED MODEL. It is a network that does not exist. It has three columns of six dots each, densely wired together in grey. Each dot is a neuron, and in this imagined network every neuron is exactly one [[feature]] — one interpretable thing, cleanly separated from everything else. Nothing is shared, nothing is mixed.

The bottom panel is labelled OBSERVED MODEL. This is the network you can actually load and run. Same three columns, but only three dots each. These are real neurons.

### How to read it

Read the picture downward, following the arrows. There is one arrow per column, and each carries the same operation: the six idealized units of that column are pushed down into the three real units below it.

Six things into three slots is the whole point. In three dimensions you can only have three mutually orthogonal directions, so six directions cannot all be perpendicular; some pairs must overlap. The figure's middle caption names the compromise — the idealized neurons are *projected* onto the real network as "almost orthogonal" vectors over the neurons. This is [[superposition]], and the mechanism the paper proposes for it is [[noisy-simulation]]: a small network approximately simulating a larger, sparser one.

### Why the packing is tolerable, and what it costs

Two properties make the overlap survivable. First, [[feature-sparsity]]: on any given datapoint only a few features are active, so most overlapping pairs are never lit at the same time. Second, high dimensionality: the number of directions you can fit at small pairwise angles grows very fast with the number of dimensions, far faster than the dimension itself.

The cost is [[interference]]. Reading a feature off its almost-orthogonal direction also picks up a little of every other feature sharing space with it.

Now read the picture upward. One bottom dot lies along several top-panel feature directions, so it fires for several unrelated things. That is [[polysemanticity]] — a consequence of the projection, not a separate fact about neurons.

The panel is an illustration of a hypothesis, not a measurement; the 6-to-3 squeeze is drawn for legibility, and the real ratio the paper works with is far larger.

terms.definition: The label on the top panel. It names a network that is not observed and may not exist as a literal object — the larger, sparser network that the real one is hypothesized to be approximating.
The label on the bottom panel. It names the network that actually exists and can be run — here standing in for the paper's one-layer transformer and its MLP layer.

In the top panel's caption, a feature that occupies one unit all by itself, with no sharing. Every neuron in the hypothetical model is one of these, which is what makes that model interpretable neuron by neuron.
Neurons. In the top panel each dot is simultaneously a neuron and a feature; in the bottom panel each dot is a real neuron that may carry parts of several features.
Connections, i.e. weights between units in adjacent columns. They are drawn dense and unlabelled — the picture is about how many units there are and what they mean, not about specific weight values.
Successive layers of each cartoon network, three in each panel. They exist only to make the drawing look like a network; nothing in the figure depends on there being three.
The mapping from the hypothetical model to the observed one, one arrow per column. They run downward, meaning the larger network is expressed inside the smaller one, not recovered from it.

The word set in orange in the middle caption. It means the idealized neurons are written as vectors in the smaller network's activation space — a linear map into fewer dimensions than there were units.
Named in the first caption line. The claim that networks want to represent more features than they have neurons, and do so by giving each feature its own direction rather than its own neuron.
The bolded phrase in the first caption line. The claim that the observed network's computation approximately reproduces what a much bigger, much sparser network would compute.

The phrase in the middle caption, in scare quotes in the original. Each feature is a vector spread across many neurons, and any two such vectors have a small but nonzero dot product because there is not room for them all to be perpendicular.
The bolded phrase in the bottom caption. It restates what the arrows do: many feature directions are compressed into an activation space with fewer dimensions than there are features.

The bottom caption's closing word. What the projection looks like if you examine one real neuron: it responds to a mixture of apparently unrelated things, because several feature directions have weight on it.
The phrase from the sentence that introduces this figure. The simulation is noisy because the packing is imperfect — the larger network is reproduced approximately, not exactly.
Not drawn, but the property that makes the packing work: only a small number of features are active on any one datapoint, so most overlapping pairs are rarely on together.

Not drawn, but the price of the packing: because feature directions are not orthogonal, activating one feature slightly activates others, and reading one off its direction picks up traces of the rest.

numbers.meaning: Dots per column in the top panel — the number of features in the hypothetical disentangled network's layer. Chosen for legibility, not measured; it just needs to exceed the bottom panel's count.

Dots per column in the bottom panel — the number of real neurons available to hold those six features. In three dimensions at most three directions can be mutually orthogonal, so six directions must overlap.

The implied expansion ratio, 6 features into 3 neurons. This is the figure's illustration of overcompleteness — more directions than dimensions — at the smallest ratio that still makes the point visible.
Layers drawn in each panel. This number carries no argument; the figure would say the same thing with one column or ten.
One orange arrow per column, indicating the projection applies at every layer rather than at one special place.
Not in the figure, but what the bottom panel stands for in the paper: the MLP of the one-layer transformer under study has 512 neurons, and this is the space into which features must be packed.
Not in the figure. The expansion factor the paper mainly works with when it fits a dictionary to those 512 activations, giving 4,096 features — a far bigger squeeze than the drawn 2×.
Not in the figure. The largest expansion the paper runs, 131,072 features over 512 neurons, indicating how much larger the hypothesized top panel may be than the drawing suggests.
